Part 1 Objectives

  1. Describe the general features of chronic interstitial lung disease including the pathology of the major categories (fibrosing, granulomatous, smoking related, and eosinophilic) and the diseases in each category
  2. Describe the differences between usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) and nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP)
  3. Describe cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP)
  4. Describe the chronic pulmonary manifestations of systemic collagen vascular disease, including Caplan syndrome
  5. Describe coal worker pneumoconiosis, including the various forms and the pathologic findings
  6. Describe the clinical presentation, gross pathology, and histology of silicosis
  7. Describe asbestos-related diseases/pathologic changes, and the role of chrysotile vs. amphibole fibers
PART 1 — Interstitial Fibrosis, Pneumoconioses & Asbestos

1. General Features of Restrictive Lung Disease

ClinicalProgressive dyspnea; non-productive cough (no mucus hyperplasia component, unlike obstructive disease); dry crackles
Key mediatorTGF-β is frequently a main contributor to the fibrosis
LaboratoryBoth FEV1 and FVC decreased proportionally → normal FEV1/FVC ratio
GrossCobblestone pleural surface; honeycomb change
MicroscopicFibrosis is the common shared feature across nearly all these diseases; individual conditions have their own more specific findings on top of this
Why the FEV1/FVC ratio stays normal — reasoned out — Scarring impairs the lung's ability to fill (↓ FVC) and its ability to empty (↓ FEV1) roughly equally, so the ratio between them stays close to normal — the opposite pattern from obstructive disease, where FVC is preserved but FEV1 is disproportionately reduced.
ARDS as an acute restrictive disease — Hyaline membrane formation (the protein layered on the alveolar septa in ARDS) can be thought of as an acute restrictive process: it impairs the lung's ability to fill in the same conceptual way chronic fibrosis does, just over hours-to-days instead of months-to-years.

Major Categories & Their Diseases

CategoryDiseases
FibrosingUsual interstitial pneumonia (UIP)/idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF); nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP); cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP); collagen vascular disease-associated; pneumoconiosis; therapy-related
GranulomatousSarcoidosis; hypersensitivity pneumonitis
EosinophilicLöffler syndrome; drug-related allergies
Smoking-relatedRespiratory bronchiolitis; desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP)

Complications

Pulmonary hypertension → cor pulmonale (right-sided heart failure). Scarring destroys alveolar septa and the blood vessels running through them — fewer vascular channels means the right heart has to generate more pressure to push the same cardiac output through the lungs, and over time it fails from the added strain.

USMLE-Style Question

A patient with several years of progressive dyspnea and dry cough is found to have pulmonary function tests showing FEV1 60% predicted and FVC 58% predicted. Which of the following best explains why the FEV1/FVC ratio remains near-normal in this patient?

A. Both the ability to fill and the ability to empty the lungs are proportionally impaired by scarring
B. The lung is unable to empty but fills normally
C. Airway resistance is markedly increased
D. Elastic recoil is selectively lost
E. Goblet cell hyperplasia is compensating for reduced airflow
Answer: A. In restrictive lung disease, fibrosis/scarring reduces both FVC (ability to fill) and FEV1 (ability to empty) roughly proportionally, keeping the FEV1/FVC ratio close to normal — unlike obstructive disease, where FVC is preserved but FEV1 is disproportionately reduced.

2. UIP/IPF vs. NSIP

Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis / Usual Interstitial Pneumonia

FeatureDetail
DemographicsMale > female; >50 years of age; associated with smoking and other environmental exposures (fumes from metal, wood dust)
EtiologyNot fully understood — repeated injury; mutations of telomerase, MUC5B, and surfactant genes have been implicated
GrossCobblestone pleural surface; honeycomb change
MicroscopicFibroblastic foci (acute change) and fibrosis (chronic change) — temporal heterogeneity: lesions of different ages side by side
Why telomerase/surfactant gene mutations make sense here — Telomerase mutations can accelerate cellular aging, pushing tissue toward an "end-stage" fibrotic appearance sooner. Surfactant gene mutations remove some of the protective/anti-fibrotic function surfactant normally provides — without it, fibrosis can progress more readily. Neither fact needs to be memorized in isolation; both follow from what those genes normally do.
UIP — temporal heterogeneity, low power
Open, normal-appearing air spaces on the left transition into densely fibrotic tissue on the right — the chronic change. Within the fibrotic area, a paler, slightly bluish, hypocellular proliferation (a fibroblastic focus) represents the acute change. Seeing both an "old" fibrotic area and a "new" fibroblastic focus in the same field is the defining temporal heterogeneity of UIP.
Sampling pearl — UIP is notorious for starting subpleurally. A trainee's instinct might be to sample lung tissue near larger airways/vessels (where "most pathology occurs" in general), but for UIP specifically, sampling near the pleural surface is where the disease is most likely to be caught.

Honeycomb Change

Honeycomb change
Variably-sized cystic spaces, some lined by respiratory-type epithelium and containing mucus — at a glance this can look like emphysema. The giveaway is the pale pink material between the cystic spaces: that's scar, not simple tissue destruction. Grossly, the same logic applies with palpation: honeycomb change is firm because of the underlying fibrosis, while emphysema is soft and spongy because there's no fibrosis at all — complete loss of parenchyma with nothing replacing it.

Nonspecific Interstitial Pneumonia (NSIP)

AssociationOften with autoimmune disease, especially rheumatoid arthritis; also with non-smoking females in their 6th decade
PrognosisBetter than UIP
MicroscopicLesions are all of the same age (vs. UIP's mixed ages) — cellular and fibrosing variants
NSIP — interstitial fibrosis
Diffuse, relatively uniform thickening of the alveolar interstitium — everything looks like it's at the same stage, in contrast to UIP's side-by-side mix of old scar and new fibroblastic foci.
UIP vs. NSIP — the one fact to hang everything else on — UIP = lesions of different ages (temporal heterogeneity); NSIP = lesions of the same age (temporal homogeneity). Nearly every other distinguishing feature (demographics, smoking association, prognosis) can be reasoned outward from this core histologic difference.

USMLE-Style Question

A 62-year-old male smoker presents with progressive dyspnea over 18 months. Lung biopsy shows areas of dense chronic fibrosis adjacent to hypocellular, actively proliferating fibroblastic foci, with the disease most pronounced near the pleural surface. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A. Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia
B. Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia
C. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
D. Desquamative interstitial pneumonia
E. Usual interstitial pneumonia
Answer: E. The combination of temporal heterogeneity (fibroblastic foci of varying/mixed ages alongside chronic fibrosis), subpleural predominance, older male smoker demographics, and progressive dyspnea is classic for UIP/IPF.

USMLE-Style Question

A 58-year-old non-smoking woman with rheumatoid arthritis develops progressive dyspnea. Lung biopsy shows diffuse interstitial fibrosis with lesions that all appear to be of the same age throughout the specimen. Compared to UIP, this condition is associated with which of the following?

A. Worse prognosis than UIP
B. Strong association with smoking
C. Predominance in older males
D. Better prognosis than UIP
E. Temporal heterogeneity on histology
Answer: D. This describes NSIP (uniform lesion age, association with autoimmune disease and non-smoking females), which carries a better prognosis than UIP — the opposite of options A, B, C, and E, all of which describe UIP instead.

3. Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP)

Older term: bronchiolitis obliterans with organizing pneumonia (BOOP) — renamed partly because "bronchiolitis obliterans" risked confusion with the airway changes of chronic bronchitis, a completely different process.

The core concept — When ordinary pneumonia resolves, the alveolar spaces can develop organizing fibrosis as part of normal healing. That exact histologic pattern, occurring in a patient with no identifiable underlying cause (no preceding infection, no other explanation), is called cryptogenic organizing pneumonia. Same histologic pattern, different label depending purely on whether a cause is found — "cryptogenic" literally means "of hidden/unknown origin."

Pathology

  • Hypocellular (low cell number) fibrous proliferation within the airspaces — plugs of loose connective tissue called Masson bodies
  • Key distinction from UIP's fibroblastic foci: fibroblastic foci in UIP are within the alveolar septa; Masson bodies in COP are within the airspaces themselves — despite looking superficially similar, they are not the same finding
Organizing pneumonia pattern — Masson bodies
Rounded, whorled plugs of loose, hypocellular fibrous tissue filling the alveolar spaces (Masson bodies) — this specific field also shows admixed macrophages and some neutrophils, suggesting an actual resolving infectious pneumonia rather than a truly "cryptogenic" case. The histologic pattern itself, however, would look identical whether or not an underlying cause is ultimately identified — that distinction can only be made clinically, not on the slide alone.

USMLE-Style Question

A lung biopsy shows plugs of loose, hypocellular fibrous tissue filling the alveolar airspaces. The patient has no history of preceding infection, connective tissue disease, or other identifiable cause. What is the most likely diagnosis, and where exactly are the fibrous plugs located relative to UIP's characteristic lesion?

A. Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia; within the airspaces, unlike UIP's septal fibroblastic foci
B. UIP; within the alveolar septa, same location as COP's lesion
C. NSIP; within the pleura
D. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis; within the bronchiolar wall only
E. Desquamative interstitial pneumonia; within the vascular lumen
Answer: A. This is cryptogenic organizing pneumonia — the same organizing pneumonia pattern seen after resolving infection, but with no identifiable underlying cause. Its hallmark Masson bodies sit within the airspaces themselves, distinguishing them from UIP's fibroblastic foci, which are located within the alveolar septa.

4. Collagen Vascular Disease & Caplan Syndrome

DiseasePulmonary/Pleural Features
Rheumatoid arthritisPleuritis (including effusions); pneumonitis (with fibrosis); rheumatoid nodules; bronchiolitis; pulmonary hypertension. Caplan syndrome = rheumatoid nodules in the peripheral lungs of coal miners.
Systemic sclerosisPleuritis; NSIP pattern
Systemic lupus erythematosusPleuritis (including effusions); mild to severe pneumonitis
Don't memorize this table cold — reason through it — Autoimmune diseases classically cause serositis, so pleuritis/pleural effusion showing up across all three diseases isn't a coincidence to memorize separately for each — it's the same underlying serositis tendency shared by autoimmune disease generally. And because all of these are immune-mediated attacks on the body's own tissue, some degree of pneumonitis/inflammation in the lung is unsurprising across the group. What IS relatively specific: rheumatoid nodules for RA, and the NSIP pattern for systemic sclerosis.
Fair-question principle — A well-constructed exam question wouldn't ask you to distinguish these autoimmune lung findings without giving you enough clinical context (e.g., specific autoantibodies, other systemic findings) to narrow it down — there's real overlap between them on lung findings alone.

USMLE-Style Question

A 55-year-old former coal miner with a 20-year history of rheumatoid arthritis is found to have well-circumscribed nodules in the peripheral lung fields on chest imaging. What is this combination of findings called?

A. Caplan syndrome
B. Löffler syndrome
C. Mikulicz syndrome
D. Sicca syndrome
E. Churg-Strauss syndrome
Answer: A. Caplan syndrome refers to rheumatoid nodules occurring in the peripheral lungs of coal miners — a specific, well-defined combination of coal worker's pneumoconiosis and rheumatoid arthritis-associated nodules.

5. Pneumoconioses Overview

Description: lung disease caused by exposure to an inorganic or organic substance, particle, or chemical fume.

Main three (covered in depth)Carbon (coal), asbestos, silica
BerylliumCauses non-caseating granulomas — a beryllium-specific mimicker of sarcoidosis
Iron oxideSiderosis
Moldy hay / cottonByssinosis (cotton)
Tin oxideStannosis
Board framing — Casseating granulomas are classically TB; non-caseating granulomas are classically sarcoidosis — but beryllium exposure is the pneumoconiosis-specific exception worth knowing, since it produces the sarcoid-like non-caseating pattern via an inhaled particle rather than an unknown immune-mediated process.

6. Coal Worker's Pneumoconiosis

FeatureDetail
ExposureCoal miners
FormsPulmonary anthracosis (mildest — just pigment deposition); simple coal worker's pneumoconiosis (small nodules, usually asymptomatic); complicated coal worker's pneumoconiosis / progressive massive fibrosis (much more extensive, symptomatic)
Cancer riskNo increased risk — an important distinction from silicosis and asbestosis, both of which do carry increased cancer risk
Autoimmune associationRheumatoid nodules in the lung + coal exposure = Caplan syndrome
Black lung ≠ automatically sick — A lung can be diffusely blackened by carbon pigment (even quite extensively) and still not be functionally significant. Humans can oxygenate adequately on a fraction of total lung tissue (historically, entire pneumonectomies were performed as a TB treatment) — the presence of pigment tells you about exposure, not necessarily about symptomatic disease. That's the distinction between simple and complicated coal worker's pneumoconiosis.
Anthracosis isn't unique to smoking or coal mining — Any sufficiently smoky environment (e.g., a population doing extensive indoor/outdoor cooking over open fires) can blacken lung surfaces the same way. Black pigment on a lung surface at autopsy should prompt a broader exposure history, not an automatic assumption of coal mining or cigarette smoking.
Simple coal worker's pneumoconiosis
Stellate (star-shaped), spiculated black deposits — coal macules — scattered through lung tissue that otherwise looks reasonably preserved. Despite the seemingly striking appearance, this pattern by itself is typically simple coal worker's pneumoconiosis and would not necessarily be expected to produce significant symptoms.

USMLE-Style Question

A 60-year-old former coal miner is found at autopsy to have extensive black pigment deposition scattered diffusely throughout both lungs, without evidence of significant fibrotic masses. He was reportedly asymptomatic during life. Which of the following best describes his condition, and what is his associated cancer risk?

A. Simple coal worker's pneumoconiosis; no increased cancer risk
B. Complicated coal worker's pneumoconiosis; markedly increased cancer risk
C. Silicosis; increased cancer risk
D. Asbestosis; increased cancer risk
E. Progressive massive fibrosis; increased cancer risk
Answer: A. Widespread pigment deposition without significant fibrotic masses and without symptoms is consistent with simple coal worker's pneumoconiosis. Unlike silicosis and asbestosis, coal worker's pneumoconiosis carries no increased risk of cancer.

7. Silicosis

FeatureDetail
ExposureSand-blasting, mining
DistributionUpper lobes and subpleural
Cancer riskIncreased (like asbestos, unlike coal)
Other associationIncreased risk of tuberculosis
Why the TB association is worth remembering — It's not just testable trivia: knowing a silicosis patient carries increased TB risk has real practical value (e.g., prompting more frequent PPD/IGRA testing and closer monitoring) — a good example of a "random fact" that actually changes real-world management once you know it.
Silicotic nodule
A densely fibrotic nodule with a whorled ("onion-skin") collagen pattern and scattered fine dust deposition — the classic silicotic nodule.
Same field, polarized light
Under polarized light, faint bright (birefringent) specks become visible that are essentially invisible under standard illumination — this is the silica particulate material itself. The effect can be subtle enough that it takes a careful look to appreciate, which is exactly why polarization is used: it selectively brings out foreign/crystalline material that would otherwise be easy to overlook entirely.

USMLE-Style Question

A 50-year-old male sandblaster of 20 years presents with gradually progressive dyspnea and a nonproductive cough. Chest imaging shows reticulonodular densities concentrated in the upper lobes with subpleural predominance. Which of the following best describes his risk profile compared to a coal miner with a similar duration of dust exposure?

A. Lower cancer risk than the coal miner
B. Same cancer risk as the coal miner (neither has increased risk)
C. Increased risk of carcinoma only, with no difference in infection risk
D. No difference in any disease risk between silica and coal dust exposure
E. Increased risk of carcinoma and tuberculosis, unlike the coal miner
Answer: E. Unlike coal worker's pneumoconiosis (no increased cancer risk), silicosis carries an increased risk of both carcinoma and tuberculosis — a distinguishing feature worth remembering both for exams and for real clinical management (e.g., more frequent TB screening).

8. Asbestos-Related Disease

FeatureDetail
ExposureMining, insulation work (including demolition of older buildings), shipyards, railroad engine insulation
Pleural plaquesFlat, off-white plaques on the pleural surface (and diaphragm) — do NOT contain ferruginous bodies; by themselves, do not cause disease, but strongly suggest the exposure history
AsbestosisThe restrictive lung disease caused by asbestos — associated with ferruginous bodies
Other findingsPleural effusion; dense pleural adhesions (can be severe enough that the lung must be cut out of the pleural cavity rather than separated cleanly)
Asbestos exposure ≠ asbestosis — Exposure just means contact with asbestos (which by itself raises cancer risk even without causing restrictive disease). Asbestosis specifically means the patient has developed restrictive lung disease from that exposure. A patient can have pleural plaques (evidence of exposure, increased cancer risk) without ever developing asbestosis itself.
Pleural plaques
Irregular, dense, off-white fibrous plaques on the inner pleural surface. These are strongly associated with asbestos exposure (though not entirely exclusive to it — a good exposure history still matters), and by themselves do not cause disease.
Pleural plaque on the diaphragm
A discontinuous, geographic/map-like patch of fibrous plaque coating part of the diaphragmatic surface — plaques can occur here as well as on the chest wall pleura.

Asbestosis

Asbestosis — honeycomb change, gross
This looks like emphysema at a glance — numerous cystic airspaces throughout. The distinguishing test is palpation: this tissue is firm, because it's honeycomb change from fibrosis, not true emphysematous destruction (which would feel soft and spongy). Same visual trap, same resolution, as UIP's honeycomb change in Section 2.

Ferruginous Bodies

Ferruginous body
A straight, segmented, golden-brown rod with beaded/dumbbell-shaped ends — a macrophage's attempt to wall off and neutralize an inhaled fiber it cannot otherwise clear, by coating it in iron and protein. The straight shape corresponds to an amphibole fiber (see below) — this is the single most classic, must-recognize image for asbestos exposure, and one worth being able to pick out even in a busy field on a real slide, not just a clean teaching photo.

Fiber Types

Chrysotile (serpentine)Curved/coiled shape — impacts higher up in the airway, where mucociliary clearance can remove it more effectively. Most common fiber type, but the least damaging of the two.
AmphiboleStraight shape — travels much farther down into the parenchyma and, once in the alveolar spaces, is very difficult to clear. Less common than chrysotile, but drives most of the disease burden.

USMLE-Style Question

Autopsy of a former shipyard worker reveals dense pleural adhesions requiring the lung to be dissected free from the chest wall, along with straight, golden-brown, iron-encrusted rod-shaped structures on lung histology. Which fiber type is most directly responsible for these histologic findings, and why does this fiber type reach the alveoli more readily than the alternative?

A. Amphibole; its straight shape allows it to travel farther into the parenchyma before mucociliary clearance can act
B. Chrysotile; its curved shape allows deeper penetration
C. Chrysotile; it is cleared exclusively by pleural macrophages
D. Amphibole; it dissolves in alveolar fluid before triggering a reaction
E. Neither fiber type reaches the alveoli; only the pleura is affected
Answer: A. Amphibole fibers are straight, allowing them to travel much farther into the pulmonary parenchyma and alveolar spaces than the curved (serpentine) chrysotile fibers, which tend to impact higher in the airway where they can still be cleared by the mucociliary escalator. Amphibole fibers, once in the alveoli, are very difficult to clear — producing the classic ferruginous bodies.

10. Part 1 Lecture Case

Lecture Case

A 52-year-old male presents with shortness of breath that developed gradually over 1–2 years. His past medical history includes GERD. He worked as a sandblaster for 20 years. Chest X-ray reveals reticular and finely nodular densities in the upper lobes. Which mediator is most directly involved in the development of this disease process?

A. IgE
B. Interleukin-5
C. Complement C5a
D. TGF-β
E. Angiotensin-converting enzyme
Answer: D. The sandblasting history and upper-lobe reticulonodular pattern point to silicosis, a fibrosing restrictive lung disease. As with essentially all fibrosing restrictive lung diseases, TGF-β is the main mediator driving the fibrotic response.

11. Asbestos Add-On & Drug/Therapy-Related Disease

Worth repeating — With malignant pleural mesothelioma, the working assumption should be asbestos exposure until proven otherwise — it is essentially the only cause outside rare exceptions. Asbestos-exposed patients are also at increased risk of bronchogenic carcinoma (squamous cell carcinoma has been specifically observed in this setting).
Smoking alone: ~10x cancer risk. Asbestos alone: ~5x cancer risk. Both together: ~50x risk (synergistic, not merely additive)

Exact multipliers vary somewhat between sources/studies — an exam question is unlikely to demand a precise number, but the synergistic relationship (far greater than simply adding 10x + 5x) is the high-yield, testable point.

Drug/Therapy-Related Restrictive Lung Disease

AmiodaroneThe most commonly encountered drug-related cause at autopsy in this lecturer's experience — "cardiologists love it, everybody else hates it," reflecting its efficacy against arrhythmias weighed against a real burden of extracardiac toxicity, including the lung
Radiation therapyDirect tissue damage → scarring, following the same general fibrosis mechanism as other restrictive lung diseases
ChemotherapyBleomycin, busulfan
Amiodarone-associated interstitial lung disease — gross
The pleural surface here is distinctly bumpy/irregular rather than smooth — an immediately visible abnormality even before sectioning. (This particular image was also used to reinforce that two visible lobes does not automatically mean "left lung" — this is actually the right lung; lobe-counting alone can mislead, as covered in Part 1's left-vs-right discussion.)
Amiodarone-associated interstitial lung disease — histology
Recognizable air spaces are present, but the walls between them are much thicker and more fibrotic than normal lung — the histologic correlate of drug-induced restrictive lung disease. As with the other conditions in this unit, gross palpation would reveal this lung to be firmer than normal because of the underlying scarring.

USMLE-Style Question

A patient with a history of chronic atrial fibrillation treated for several years with an antiarrhythmic medication develops progressive dyspnea and is found to have bilateral pulmonary fibrosis on imaging. Which medication is most likely responsible?

A. Metoprolol
B. Digoxin
C. Warfarin
D. Amiodarone
E. Diltiazem
Answer: D. Amiodarone is a well-known cause of drug-induced pulmonary fibrosis/interstitial lung disease, and is the most commonly encountered drug-related restrictive lung disease seen at autopsy according to this lecture — a real-world reflection of the drug's efficacy for arrhythmias being weighed against a meaningful burden of extracardiac (including pulmonary) toxicity.

USMLE-Style Question

A patient with known heavy asbestos exposure from years of shipyard work continued smoking one pack of cigarettes per day for the same duration. Compared to either exposure alone, his risk of developing bronchogenic carcinoma is best described as which of the following?

A. Simply additive (approximately the sum of each individual risk)
B. No different from either exposure alone
C. Protective — combined exposure reduces overall risk
D. Relevant only to mesothelioma risk, not bronchogenic carcinoma
E. Synergistic — dramatically greater than the sum of the two individual risks
Answer: E. Asbestos exposure and smoking act synergistically on bronchogenic carcinoma risk — roughly 10x from smoking alone and 5x from asbestos alone, but approximately 50x when combined — far exceeding what simple addition of the two individual risks would predict.

12. Sarcoidosis

FeatureDetail
EtiologyUnknown — genuinely a strength for exam purposes, since a question can't reasonably ask you to identify a cause that isn't known
PathogenesisGenetically predisposed individual with immune dysregulation involving TH1 T cells (contrast with TH2 cells in asthma)
General featuresNon-caseating granulomas; Schaumann bodies; asteroid bodies
TH1 vs. TH2 — a useful contrast to lock in — Sarcoidosis is driven by TH1 T cells; asthma (Part 3 of the obstructive lung disease series) is driven by TH2 cells. Having one clean example of each helps anchor which immune pathway goes with which disease pattern.

Organ Involvement

LungHilar lymphadenopathy first; can progress to involve the pulmonary parenchyma with fibrosis — disease can be staged by how far it has progressed, with parenchymal fibrosis being the more advanced/consequential stage
SkinErythema nodosum (no granulomas — a hemorrhagic-appearing reactive process); can also have subcutaneous granulomas (which DO have granulomas)
Eye/lacrimal glandsIritis, choroiditis, optic nerve involvement; sicca syndrome (dry eyes/mouth); Mikulicz syndrome = combined uveal (eye) + parotid (salivary gland) involvement
HeartCan mimic remote MI-type scarring of the myocardium, but without significant coronary artery disease to explain it — an important distinguishing clue
OtherSpleen, liver, bone marrow (the adrenal gland is reportedly spared, though this is less certain/less commonly confirmed)
MetabolicHypercalcemia/hypercalciuria — from macrophages within granulomas activating vitamin D, which drives bone mineralization (↑ serum calcium/phosphate handling)
Lab markerElevated ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme), with the degree of elevation roughly proportional to disease burden — potentially useful for monitoring treatment response
Hilar lymphadenopathy
Posterior view of the tracheal bifurcation, showing markedly enlarged, cobblestone-nodular lymph nodes just below it — the classic first site of sarcoid involvement in the chest.
Non-caseating granuloma
A well-circumscribed collection of epithelioid histiocytes (enlarged cells with abundant cytoplasm and small nuclei) — with no central necrosis, distinguishing it from the caseating granulomas of tuberculosis. Note that giant cells are not required to call something a granuloma — the epithelioid histiocyte collection itself is the defining feature, though multinucleated giant cells are frequently also present.
Asteroid body
A star-shaped (asteroid), radiating eosinophilic inclusion within a multinucleated giant cell — seen in granulomatous inflammation broadly, and specifically listed as a sarcoidosis-associated finding in major pathology references. (A minor point of professional disagreement exists over how specific this finding is to sarcoidosis vs. other granulomatous processes — but for testing purposes, the standard reference association is what matters.)
Schaumann body
A dark, basophilic (bluish), laminated calcified concretion within granulomatous inflammation — less commonly encountered on individual slides than asteroid bodies, but still a classic listed sarcoidosis finding.
Multiple pulmonary granulomas
Several discrete, well-formed granulomas scattered through the lung parenchyma — illustrating the multifocal pattern of granulomatous involvement typical of sarcoidosis before it progresses to confluent fibrosis.

USMLE-Style Question

A patient with biopsy-proven sarcoidosis is found to have an elevated serum calcium level. Which mechanism best explains this finding?

A. Direct granuloma-mediated bone resorption
B. Macrophages within granulomas activate vitamin D, increasing calcium absorption
C. Ectopic parathyroid hormone secretion by granulomas
D. Renal tubular calcium wasting from granulomatous nephritis
E. Hypoalbuminemia falsely elevating the measured calcium
Answer: B. In sarcoidosis, macrophages within non-caseating granulomas produce active vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), which increases intestinal calcium absorption and can lead to hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria — a distinct mechanism from primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy-related hypercalcemia.

USMLE-Style Question

A patient with sarcoidosis develops dry eyes, dry mouth, and swelling of the parotid glands along with uveitis. What is this specific combination of findings called?

A. Caplan syndrome
B. Löffler syndrome
C. Churg-Strauss syndrome
D. Sicca syndrome alone
E. Mikulicz syndrome
Answer: E. Mikulicz syndrome refers to the combination of uveal (eye) and parotid (salivary gland) involvement in sarcoidosis — a specific named pattern distinct from sicca syndrome (dry eyes/mouth) alone, which can occur without the parotid component being specifically named this way.

13. Sarcoidosis — Organ Involvement & Complications

Beyond the lung, skin, and eyes, sarcoid granulomas have been documented in a wide range of organs — the renal and hepatic examples below simply illustrate that this is a genuinely systemic, multi-organ disease process, not one confined to the chest.

Cardiopulmonary Complications

As with any restrictive/fibrosing lung process, advanced pulmonary parenchymal sarcoidosis can progress to pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular strain. In severe cases, the right ventricular wall thickness can become nearly equal to the left ventricle's — a dramatic illustration of just how much extra work the right heart is forced to do once enough pulmonary vasculature has been obliterated by fibrosis.

Right ventricular hypertrophy from advanced pulmonary sarcoidosis
Heart cross-section (left) showing right ventricular wall thickness approaching that of the left ventricle — a striking degree of right heart strain. The accompanying lung specimen (right) is extensively scarred; in a real case this severe, the lung tissue can be difficult to even cut through because of how dense the fibrosis has become. This pairing illustrates the direct causal link between advanced restrictive lung disease and cor pulmonale discussed conceptually back in Part 1.

Erythema Nodosum

Erythema nodosum
Raised, tender, reddish-purple nodular lesions, classically along the shins — a reactive, hemorrhagic-appearing skin process (no granulomas present histologically, despite occurring in a granulomatous systemic disease). Recognizing this lesion pattern together with hilar lymphadenopathy on imaging is a classic way sarcoidosis is identified clinically.

USMLE-Style Question

A pathology resident examines tissue from an autopsy of a 37-year-old man who died after 10 days in the hospital following a motor vehicle accident. Hilar lymphadenopathy and focal firm regions of pulmonary parenchyma are identified. Microscopic exam of the firm regions and lymph nodes reveals non-caseating granulomas, negative acid-fast stains, laminated concretions, and eosinophilic stellate inclusions within giant cells. Which cell type is most centrally involved in the pathogenesis of this disease process?

A. TH2 helper T cells
B. B lymphocytes
C. Eosinophils
D. Mast cells
E. TH1 helper T cells
Answer: E. This is sarcoidosis (non-caseating granulomas, negative AFB stain ruling out TB, Schaumann bodies [laminated concretions], and asteroid bodies [eosinophilic stellate inclusions in giant cells]). The pathogenesis centrally involves TH1 T cells in a genetically predisposed individual with immune dysregulation.

14. Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis

As the name implies: a hypersensitivity reaction to something inhaled. Many distinct named forms exist based on the specific exposure — you don't need to memorize every name, but recognizing the pattern (occupational/hobby inhalational exposure → lung reaction) is the key skill.

Farmer's lungThermophilic actinomycetes from dust in hay
Pigeon breeder's lungProteins from birds
Humidifier lungThermophilic bacteria in heated water reservoirs
The recurring lesson of this whole lecture series — Ask patients about their occupation and hobbies. The same underlying pattern (inhaled organic/inorganic material → lung disease) shows up across pneumoconioses, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and more — exposure history is doing real diagnostic work here, not just filling out a chart.

Pathogenesis & Pathology

  • Immunologic — increased CD4 and CD8 cells and antibodies; the precise mechanistic details are still being worked out, though the overall immune-mediated nature is established
  • Pathology: peribronchiolar granulomas (i.e., farther down the airway than "peribronchial"); interstitial inflammation; late stage → interstitial fibrosis and honeycombing (converging on the same general endpoint as other chronic restrictive lung diseases)
AcuteFever, dyspnea, cough, ↑ white blood cell count; PFTs show a restrictive pattern
ChronicProgressive respiratory failure with dyspnea and cyanosis; decreased total lung capacity and compliance
Granulomas here look different from sarcoid's — Hypersensitivity pneumonitis granulomas are classically described as ill-defined/poorly formed, located peribronchiolarly. Don't expect the same crisp, well-circumscribed appearance as a sarcoid granuloma — if a field looks vaguely granulomatous but loosely organized, in the right clinical context (exposure history, restrictive PFTs), that's consistent with hypersensitivity pneumonitis rather than a failure to find a "real" granuloma.
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis — ill-defined granulomas
Loosely-formed cellular aggregates within the interstitium, lacking the sharp, well-circumscribed border of a classic (e.g., sarcoid) granuloma. This "ill-defined" quality is a real and expected feature of hypersensitivity pneumonitis, not a sign that something was mis-sampled or mis-read.

USMLE-Style Question

A 31-year-old male develops sudden fever, cough, and shortness of breath about six hours after starting a new job cleaning central heating and air ducts. He has had no sick contacts. Which of the following pathologic findings would be most characteristic of his condition?

A. Caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli
B. Extensive pulmonary edema with normal cardiac function
C. Peribronchiolar, ill-defined granulomas
D. Hyaline membranes with diffuse alveolar damage
E. Curschmann spirals and Charcot-Leyden crystals
Answer: C. This is acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis ("humidifier lung"/duct-cleaning-related exposure) — the acute onset within hours of a new inhalational exposure, with fever, dyspnea, and cough, is classic. Pathologically, ill-defined peribronchiolar granulomas are the expected finding, distinct from the well-formed granulomas of TB or sarcoidosis, and distinct from a purely cardiogenic edema picture.

15. Pulmonary Eosinophilia

Simple pulmonary eosinophilia (Löffler syndrome)Caused by migrating helminth larvae (often Strongyloides)
Secondary eosinophiliaAsthma, drug allergy, Churg-Strauss syndrome (a vasculitis with a prominent eosinophilic component)
Idiopathic chronic eosinophilic pneumoniaA diagnosis of exclusion — everything else must be ruled out first; not well understood mechanistically
Acute eosinophilic pneumoniaRapid onset of fever, dyspnea, and respiratory failure — a genuinely serious, potentially rapidly fatal condition

Acute Eosinophilic Pneumonia — Details

  • Diffuse infiltrates on imaging
  • Bronchoalveolar lavage: prominence of eosinophils
  • Histology: diffuse alveolar damage (the same underlying pattern as ARDS — this condition can present and behave like an eosinophil-driven form of ARDS)
Reasoning through severity/presentation, generally — For any of these lung conditions, the same logical framework applies: acute processes tend to present rapidly, often with fever (if inflammation is involved), and can be more immediately dangerous (up to respiratory failure); chronic processes develop more gradually and are picked up as progressive symptoms over time. Applying this lens consistently is often more useful than memorizing each condition's presentation as an isolated fact.

USMLE-Style Question

A patient presents with rapid onset of fever, dyspnea, and respiratory failure. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows a marked prominence of eosinophils, and lung biopsy shows diffuse alveolar damage. Which condition does this describe?

A. Idiopathic chronic eosinophilic pneumonia
B. Löffler syndrome
C. Acute eosinophilic pneumonia
D. Churg-Strauss syndrome without pulmonary involvement
E. Simple pulmonary eosinophilia
Answer: C. Acute eosinophilic pneumonia presents with rapid-onset fever, dyspnea, and respiratory failure, with eosinophil-rich bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and a diffuse alveolar damage pattern on histology — essentially an eosinophil-driven variant of the ARDS/DAD picture.

16. Smoking-Related Restrictive Disease

Three entities, representing a spectrum of increasing severity from the same underlying smoking-related insult.

Pulmonary Anthracosis

Normal lung surface should appear pink/tan. Black pigment deposition on the pleural surface — most often from smoking, though other heavily polluted environments can cause it too. By itself, this typically does not indicate underlying disease (no emphysema or other pathology necessarily present alongside it).

Pulmonary anthracosis
Black pigment deposition tracing the lobular pattern of the pleural surface — a purely pigmentary finding most commonly from smoking, contrasted against the normal pink-tan appearance the lung surface should otherwise have.

Smoker's (Respiratory) Bronchiolitis

Pigmented macrophages accumulate around the bronchioles. By itself, not necessarily symptomatic — but this can progress toward fibrosis and a more genuinely interstitial lung disease pattern.

Respiratory bronchiolitis
A cluster of pigment-laden (tan-brown) macrophages around the bronchiole, confirmed as smoking-related pigment rather than the hemosiderin of chronic congestive heart failure (distinguishable with iron stains when the clinical picture is ambiguous). Progression toward the accompanying alveolar septal fibrosis marks the transition from a purely bronchiolar finding toward more genuine interstitial lung disease.

Desquamative Interstitial Pneumonia (DIP)

A major accumulation of alveolar macrophages essentially filling the airspaces diffusely. Essentially exclusively a disease of cigarette smokers — a genuinely characteristic exposure association.

Desquamative interstitial pneumonia
Essentially every alveolar airspace in the field is filled with macrophages — a diffuse, striking pattern at low power. This condition is characteristically seen almost exclusively in cigarette smokers.
The smoking-related spectrum, in order of severity — Anthracosis (pigment only, no real disease) → Respiratory bronchiolitis (pigmented macrophages + early fibrosis, still often asymptomatic) → DIP (diffuse macrophage filling of airspaces, genuine interstitial lung disease). Same exposure, progressively more significant pathology.

USMLE-Style Question

A 55-year-old lifelong smoker undergoes lung biopsy for progressive dyspnea. Nearly every alveolar airspace in the specimen is diffusely filled with macrophages, without significant fibrosis elsewhere. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A. Pulmonary anthracosis
B. Respiratory bronchiolitis
C. Desquamative interstitial pneumonia
D. Usual interstitial pneumonia
E. Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis
Answer: C. Diffuse filling of essentially every alveolar airspace with macrophages, in a smoker, is the classic description of desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP) — a condition seen essentially exclusively in cigarette smokers.

17. Other Causes: Musculoskeletal Disorders

Not every restrictive lung disease originates within the lung parenchyma itself. Severe spinal deformity can mechanically restrict the chest wall enough to produce a functionally restrictive picture, even with structurally normal lung tissue.

Scoliosis
Lateral (left-right) curvature of the vertebral column, visible on this chest film.
Kyphosis
Forward curvature of the thoracic spine, seen here on a lateral projection.
A real clinical example worth remembering — A patient with severe kyphoscoliosis was ventilator-dependent purely because her twisted vertebral column mechanically prevented effective breathing — her lung parenchyma itself was otherwise perfectly normal. This is a genuinely restrictive physiologic picture with no primary intrinsic lung pathology at all, illustrating that "restrictive lung disease" as a functional category is broader than the parenchymal diseases covered elsewhere in this lecture series.

18. Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis

FeatureDetail
EtiologyDefect in macrophages or in granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) signaling
PathogenesisAccumulation of surfactant (a protein-lipid material) within the airspaces — macrophages normally clear surfactant turnover, and when that clearance fails, it simply piles up
FormsAutoimmune (antibodies against GM-CSF — the most common form); secondary (to another condition); congenital (inherited deficiency)
Secondary causesSilicosis, lysinuric protein intolerance, immunodeficiency disorders
Clinical presentationCough with gelatinous sputum; symptoms can be present for years before diagnosis (the condition is rare enough that recognition can be significantly delayed); prone to secondary infection (the accumulated material is a good culture medium, the same theme seen with mucus plugging in other conditions); dyspnea, cyanosis; can resolve
Silica connection worth remembering — Silica exposure comes up repeatedly across this lecture series (silicosis in Part 1) and resurfaces here as a recognized secondary cause of PAP — a good example of how one exposure can plausibly contribute to more than one distinct lung disease pattern.
PAP has no fibrosis (at least initially) — Unlike most of the conditions in this lecture, PAP is a restrictive lung disease from airspace filling, not from fibrotic scarring — though fibrosis could theoretically develop over a long enough course. This is a genuine exception to the "fibrosis is the common shared feature" rule stated back in Section 1.
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis — histology
Alveolar airspaces filled with pink material that has a granular, slightly textured quality — this is the key distinguishing feature from simple pulmonary edema, where the intra-alveolar fluid is uniformly smooth and homogeneous (as seen in the ARDS/edema lecture material). At a glance, PAP material can look similar to edema fluid, but the textured character on closer inspection is the tell.

USMLE-Style Question

A patient presents with chronic cough productive of gelatinous sputum and progressive dyspnea over several years. Lung biopsy shows alveolar airspaces filled with granular, textured pink material — distinct from the smooth appearance of simple edema fluid. Antibodies against which protein are most likely to be found in the most common form of this condition?

A. Surfactant protein B
B. GM-CSF
C. α-1-antitrypsin
D. CFTR
E. Type II collagen
Answer: B. This describes pulmonary alveolar proteinosis. The most common (autoimmune) form is caused by antibodies against GM-CSF, impairing the macrophage function needed to normally clear surfactant turnover, leading to progressive accumulation of surfactant material within the alveolar airspaces.

20. Part 2 Lecture Cases

Lecture Case 1

A 31-year-old male develops sudden fever, cough, and shortness of breath about six hours after starting a new job cleaning central hot air ducts. He has not been exposed to anyone sick. What is the most characteristic finding for this disease process?

A. Bilateral spontaneous pneumothorax
B. Extensive pulmonary edema from congestive heart failure
C. Peribronchiolar ill-defined granulomas
D. Caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli
E. Curschmann spirals
Answer: C. The acute onset within hours of a new inhalational exposure (duct-cleaning) is characteristic of acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which presents more acutely than most other restrictive lung diseases discussed in this lecture series. The expected pathologic finding is ill-defined peribronchiolar granulomas. There is no history suggesting CHF, TB, or a primary pneumothorax etiology.

Lecture Case 2

A pathology resident examines autopsy tissue from a 37-year-old black male who died after 10 days in the hospital following a motor vehicle accident. Hilar lymphadenopathy and focal firm pulmonary regions are identified, showing non-caseating granulomas with negative acid-fast stains, laminated concretions, and eosinophilic stellate inclusions in giant cells. What are the laminated concretions and eosinophilic stellate inclusions called, respectively?

A. Ferruginous bodies and Curschmann spirals
B. Schaumann bodies and asteroid bodies
C. Asteroid bodies and Schaumann bodies
D. Charcot-Leyden crystals and Masson bodies
E. Psammoma bodies and Councilman bodies
Answer: B. The laminated calcified concretions are Schaumann bodies, and the eosinophilic stellate (star-shaped) inclusions within giant cells are asteroid bodies — both classic findings in sarcoidosis, seen here alongside non-caseating granulomas and hilar lymphadenopathy.

Lecture Case 3

During a day in clinic, a pulmonologist sees five patients, each with a different work or hobby exposure: one worked a vermiculite mine in Libby, Montana; one was a sandblaster; one worked in coal mines in Wyoming; one raised pigeons; one worked in an auto body shop with isocyanate exposure. All five patients share risk for which general category of disease?

A. Obstructive lung disease
B. Restrictive lung disease
C. Pulmonary embolism
D. Primary lung cancer only, with no benign disease risk
E. Bronchiectasis exclusively
Answer: B. Each exposure (asbestos from the vermiculite mine, silica from sandblasting, coal dust, bird proteins from pigeon breeding, and isocyanates from auto body work) is associated with a different specific form of restrictive lung disease — asbestosis, silicosis, coal worker's pneumoconiosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis (pigeon breeder's lung), and occupational hypersensitivity/restrictive disease from isocyanate exposure, respectively. The common thread across all five is restrictive lung disease as the general category.

Lecture Case 4

A 36-year-old male presents with slightly painful, red, raised nodules on his legs. His history is otherwise unremarkable aside from an appendectomy. Vital signs, CBC, and liver panel are normal. Chest X-ray reveals findings consistent with hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A. Systemic lupus erythematosus
B. Undiagnosed trauma
C. Angiosarcoma
D. Sarcoidosis
E. Congestive heart failure
Answer: D. The combination of erythema nodosum (the painful red raised leg nodules) and hilar lymphadenopathy is a classic presentation of sarcoidosis. There is no evidence provided for CHF, lupus (no ANA testing mentioned, and this vignette doesn't support that diagnosis), a vascular tumor, or trauma.

21. Master High-Yield Pearls (Both Parts)

  • Restrictive lung disease core physiology: ↓FEV1 and ↓FVC together → normal ratio (vs. obstructive disease's low ratio). Fibrosis is the shared histologic theme — except pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, which restricts by airspace filling rather than scarring.
  • UIP vs. NSIP — the single fact that explains everything else: different-age lesions (UIP) vs. same-age lesions (NSIP). UIP = older male smokers, worse prognosis. NSIP = autoimmune-associated, non-smoking females, better prognosis.
  • COP's Masson bodies sit in the airspaces; UIP's fibroblastic foci sit in the alveolar septa — a subtle but real distinction between two superficially similar-looking fibrotic proliferations.
  • Cancer risk differs across the pneumoconioses: coal = no increased risk; silica and asbestos = both increased. Silicosis also carries increased TB risk.
  • Asbestos exposure ≠ asbestosis — exposure alone still raises cancer risk (mesothelioma, bronchogenic carcinoma) without necessarily causing restrictive lung disease. Straight amphibole fibers (not curved chrysotile) drive most of the parenchymal disease and the classic ferruginous bodies.
  • Smoking + asbestos is synergistic (~50x), not merely additive (~15x) — a genuinely high-yield numeric relationship.
  • Sarcoidosis = unknown etiology, TH1-driven, non-caseating granulomas ± Schaumann/asteroid bodies, hilar lymphadenopathy, hypercalcemia (macrophage vitamin D activation), elevated ACE, erythema nodosum (no granulomas), and a genuinely multi-organ reach (eye, heart, liver, spleen, bone marrow).
  • Hypersensitivity pneumonitis granulomas are classically ill-defined and peribronchiolar — don't expect sarcoid's crisp circumscription. Always ask about occupational/hobby exposures — the same principle threads through pneumoconioses, HP, and beyond.
  • The smoking-related restrictive spectrum — anthracosis (pigment only) → respiratory bronchiolitis (pigment + early fibrosis) → DIP (diffuse alveolar macrophage filling, essentially exclusive to smokers).
  • Not all restrictive disease is intrinsic to the lung — severe kyphoscoliosis can produce a restrictive physiologic picture purely from chest wall mechanics, with structurally normal lung parenchyma.
  • PAP vs. pulmonary edema on histology — both can fill alveoli with pink material, but PAP's is granular/textured while edema fluid is smooth and homogeneous. Silicosis is a recognized secondary cause of PAP.
  • Recurring exam-writing philosophy stated directly by the lecturer: a fair question gives you enough clinical detail to narrow overlapping possibilities (e.g., autoimmune lung disease findings) — and image-based questions on this material are chosen to be genuinely classic/recognizable rather than obscure.
